clue.text: Hunter, perhaps, in mourning retaining black case for observation

parts.note: a hunter is a pocket watch with a hinged cover over its face, so it is one example of a timepiece
taken as written

indicators.note: retaining means keeping something held within, so the sorrow word holds the black letter inside it

parts.note: mourning is a state of sorrow or grief
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A bereaved hunter in mourning keeps hold of a black case, perhaps a gun case, while under observation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunter, perhaps' looks like a person but is the watch with a cover; 'retaining' puts B inside GRIEF after its G.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawyer holding this is instructed to observe a court case on a client's behalf without taking part.

clue.text: Every so often, cash for loan on return is welcome

indicators.note: on return means the letters picked are read in the opposite direction, from right to left
every so often signals taking letters at regular intervals, here every second letter of these three words

explanation.surface: A lender's notice: now and then, cash advanced for a loan is gladly received when paid back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every so often' picks the even letters of 'cash for loan', AHOLA, and 'on return' reads them backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hawaiian word is a greeting used to say hello and bid visitors a warm reception.

clue.text: Quietly reforming army is no mean business

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for playing quietly

indicators.note: reforming means forming again in a new shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Once the army quietly reforms, it is no longer a mean, stingy outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mean business' looks like the idiom for being serious, but here it is the business of being mean, stinginess.
explanation.definitionFit: Being mean with money is extreme thrift, and this noun names that stinginess.

clue.text: Resort where a tour's been organised

indicators.note: organised means arranged into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A seaside town where a holiday tour has been arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of 'tour's' counts as a letter here: the fodder is A TOURS BEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaside town on the Sussex coast of southern England, long popular for holidays.

clue.text: Stick flourished — and a couple of cards

parts.note: FL is fl., short for floruit, Latin for 'flourished', used of the period a person was active
A and K are the ace and king, two playing cards

explanation.surface: Someone waves a stick about and plays a pair of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' is a noun meaning criticism, as in 'taking stick', not a piece of wood.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang 'stick' means harsh criticism, the same thing as hostile comment fired at someone.

clue.text: Crime bureau having French in, for one

indicators.note: having one thing for another means a swap: the new letters take the place of the old ones
having one thing for another means a swap: the new letters take the place of the old ones

parts.note: a bureau is an office, as in a government department
I is the Roman numeral for one
en is the French word for 'in'

explanation.surface: A crime bureau whose staff include a Frenchman, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French in' is the French word for 'in', EN, which replaces the I (one) in OFFICE.
explanation.definitionFit: An unlawful act is a breach of the law, the sense of this word in legal use.

clue.text: What writer used at home: hollow keypunch with gold point

parts.note: at home means in, as in 'staying in'

indicators.note: hollow means emptied of its inside, leaving only the first and last letters of keypunch

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
N, north, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A description of what a writer used at home: a hollowed-out keypunch with a gold nib.
explanation.walkthrough: Old writers kept ink in a horn container; 'hollow keypunch' leaves K and H.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned container for ink, originally made from animal horn, held by scribes as they wrote.

clue.text: Port back in the time before WWII, say, briefly storing books

indicators.note: storing means holding something within, so the books go inside
back means the shortened word is read in reverse
briefly means cut short, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: the years before the Second World War are the prewar period, the war being an example
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A port looked back on from before the Second World War, briefly, as a place that stored books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the clipped prewar word, and 'storing' sets the New Testament books just after its first letter. Antwerp is a Belgian port, not a British one.
explanation.definitionFit: A major Belgian city on the Scheldt, one of Europe's largest seaports.

clue.text: Bronze set with old cross

parts.note: tan is a bronze, sun-darkened colour
to gel is to set, as a jelly does

explanation.surface: Bronze set into an old cross, like a piece of church metalwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like a crucifix, but it is a hybrid fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A citrus fruit bred as a hybrid of tangerine and pomelo or grapefruit, so a cross.

clue.text: Reduced expenditure, suitably from the right client

indicators.note: from the right means the letters are read in the reverse direction
reduced means cut down to a small part, so only a few letters are taken from inside these words

explanation.surface: Advice to cut spending to suit one's means, starting from the right.
explanation.walkthrough: The run RESU spans 'expenditure, suitably'; 'from the right' reads it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A customer of a service is someone who makes use of it, as a computer system's account holder does.

clue.text: Judge lacking heart, yet to hold administrative seat

parts.note: to count is to judge or consider, as in 'I count myself lucky'

indicators.note: lacking heart means the middle letter of the word is removed

parts.note: taken as written before losing its middle
to own is to hold or possess

explanation.surface: A heartless judge has yet to take hold of the seat of local government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' wants to be a noun but is the verb COUNT; 'lacking heart' goes with 'yet', leaving YT.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief town of a British shire, where its council and courts are based.

clue.text: Uncool tie not normally something the Speaker might display?

indicators.note: not normally means not in the usual form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An uncool tie is not what the Speaker of the House would normally wear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Speaker' suggests the chair of the House of Commons; the question mark says it is any speaker showing skill in diction.
explanation.definitionFit: Clear, careful diction is the skill a public orator shows when delivering words.

clue.text: Where you'll find Athene's the idiot!

parts.note: where you find something is the place it is in, so this phrase supplies the little word for being inside

indicators.note: the word 'the' names the three letters to lift out of the goddess's name, since they sit in the middle of it

parts.note: Athene is the Greek goddess of wisdom, her name taken as written

explanation.surface: Somewhere you will meet the goddess Athene, the fool.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one riddle: the word 'the' is found inside 'Athene', in A and NE. 'idiot' is an adjective here, as in 'idiot remarks'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something silly or senseless is foolish, the behaviour of a fool or simpleton.

clue.text: Which unlikely race winner filled the kitty

explanation.surface: A riddle about the slowcoach who won the race and scooped the prize money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kitty' looks like a pot of money a winner takes, but it is a cat with mottled fur. The tortoise of Aesop's fable beat the hare.
explanation.definitionFit: The fable's slow victor of the race against the hare lived inside its hard casing; and a cat with mottled black and orange fur is so called.

clue.text: Don, a shade upset, pondered Queen's comment?

parts.note: to don clothes is to put them on and wear them

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so these letters read in reverse

parts.note: a shade is a tone of colour
to have mused is to have pondered

explanation.surface: Don, a bit upset, mulled over what the monarch said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a name or a university fellow; it is the verb meaning put on. A + TONE upset gives ENOTA.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous phrase of disapproval attributed to Victoria, using the royal plural.

clue.text: Toe, not foot, honks!

indicators.note: in a down clue the foot is the bottom, so not foot means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a tootsy is a childish word for a toe

explanation.surface: A toe rather than a whole foot gets stubbed, and someone honks in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foot' looks like the body part paired with 'Toe', but it means the bottom letter of the word in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A horn sounding short blasts does this, the same as honking.

clue.text: Crackpot in old car following van

indicators.note: following means the old car comes after the front word

parts.note: the van is the front or forefront, the head of something
a banger is British slang for an old, battered car

explanation.surface: A crackpot in an old car follows a van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'van' looks like a vehicle beside 'old car', but it is the vanguard, the head. A banger is British slang for an old car.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a wild-eyed eccentric or fanatic, someone mad.

clue.text: Powerful drink being lifted, writer strains?

indicators.note: lifted in a down clue means raised up, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a pen is a writer, something you write with
strains are snatches of music, a tune

explanation.surface: A strong drink is raised while a writer strains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Powerful drink' looks like strong liquor; 'the drink' is slang for the sea, and the being with power over it is its god.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of the sea, a deity ruling the waters.

clue.text: American partner one's secured to manage land in Africa

indicators.note: secured means holding something fast within it, so the managing word goes inside

parts.note: bud, from buddy, is American slang for a friend or partner
to run something is to manage it
I is one, the Roman numeral, with the 's meaning 'has'

explanation.surface: An American's partner has secured the right to manage some land in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'secured' makes the American pal plus one hold the managing word, which sits between the U and the D.
explanation.definitionFit: A small landlocked country in east-central Africa, bordering Rwanda and Tanzania.

clue.text: Wader one put on twice

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
bis is Latin for twice, used in music to call for a repeat

explanation.surface: A person wearing waders has to put them on twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wader' looks like a boot but is a long-legged bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-legged bird with a curved bill that feeds in marshes and shallows.

clue.text: Pay London college receiving nothing repeatedly for free

parts.note: to foot a bill is to pay it

indicators.note: receiving means taking something in, so the circles go inside the college letters

parts.note: LSE is the London School of Economics

indicators.note: repeatedly here means the letter is given twice

parts.note: O, the figure zero, is nothing

explanation.surface: A London college pays for students who get nothing again and again for free.
explanation.walkthrough: LSE takes in OO to give LOOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Unattached and able to go anywhere, without ties, the sense of being at liberty.

clue.text: Colour range on American ladies' skin in the Scottish air

parts.note: to dye is to colour
ken is range of knowledge or sight
john is American slang for a toilet, the ladies' room
peel is the skin of a fruit

explanation.surface: Colour range on an American woman's skin in the Scottish climate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'air' is a tune, not the weather. The song is a Cumbrian hunting song, but its opening 'd'ye ken' (do you know) is Scots-sounding dialect.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional song about the huntsman John Peel, whose title is phrased in northern dialect.

clue.text: Largely fat-free sauces: no dressing for us!

parts.note: skinny describes a low-fat version, as in a skinny latte made with skimmed milk
dips are thick sauces for dipping food in

explanation.surface: A menu note on low-fat sauces, and a refusal of salad dressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressing' looks like salad dressing beside the sauces, but it means putting on clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathing naked are swims taken without a costume, so with no clothes on.

clue.text: Supplied paper to cover it, due to cracks

indicators.note: to cover means to go around, so the newspaper letters sit either side of it

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times, a newspaper
taken as written

indicators.note: cracks means breaks apart, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Paper was supplied to cover something because of cracks.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper's two letters wrap round 'it', and 'cracks' rearranges 'due to' into the closing letters EDOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Equipped with everything needed, as a ship or expedition is furnished for its purpose.

clue.text: Rider in mask endlessly following behind

indicators.note: following means the trimmed mask comes after the supporting word

parts.note: to be behind someone is to back them, to be pro them

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a visor is a mask or shield for the face

explanation.surface: A rider in a mask, but missing its end, follows on behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rider' looks like a horseman; it is a clause added to a document. 'behind' means supporting, PRO.
explanation.definitionFit: A condition attached to an agreement, like an added clause qualifying a document.

clue.text: No homeowners, but X number of colonists?

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral ten
ants live in colonies, so they are colonists

explanation.surface: Not homeowners, but some colonists of an unknown number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'X number' looks like an unknown quantity, but X is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Renters occupy property owned by a landlord, so they do not own where they live.

clue.text: Turned up tips for the best toheroa: "souper" so to speak

indicators.note: turned up in a down clue means the letters are read from bottom to top
tips are ends, so the last letter of each of these words is taken

explanation.surface: A gourmet's verdict on toheroa soup: it is the best, or 'souper' as people say.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letters of 'the best toheroa souper so' are ETARO, which 'Turned up' reverses. Toheroa is a New Zealand shellfish made into soup.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver a formal speech, holding forth like a public speaker.

clue.text: Game personnel getting one running between German banks

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game
HR, human resources, is the personnel department

explanation.surface: Game staff get someone to run between German banks, as if shuttling cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' looks like financial houses, but they are riverbanks.
explanation.definitionFit: A river in western Germany, a tributary of the Rhine, flowing between its banks.
